title: Does God govern even sin?
source_text: Διὰ δὲ τὰ ἀνωτέρω πολλὰ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἡμῖν εἰρημένα οὐ χρὴ νῦν παλιλλογεῖν πρὸς τὸ ὅτι μὲν οὖν αὐτοὶ διελέγχονται σαφῶς οὐ θεὸν ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ δαίμονα, ἀλλὰ νεκρὸν σέβοντες. τοῦτο μὲν αὐτίκα διὰ τοῦτο παραλιπόντες ἴδωμεν τὰς ἑξῆς τοῦ Κέλσου λέξεις, ἐν αἷς φησι· πρότερον δὲ ἐρήσομαι. διὰ τί δαίμονας οὐ θεραπευτέον; οὐ πάντα μέντοι κατὰ γνώμην διοικεῖται τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ πᾶσα ἐξ ἐκείνου πρόνοια; καὶ ὅ τι περ ἂν (ᾖ) ἐν τοῖς ὅλοις, εἴτε θεοῦ ἔργον εἴτ᾿ ἀγγέλων εἴτ᾿ ἄλλων δαιμόνων εἴτε ἡρώων, πάντα ταῦτα ἔχει νόμον ἐκ τοῦ μεγίστου θεοῦ, τέτακται δὲ ἐφ᾿ ἑκάστῳ δύναμιν λαχὼν ὅστις ἠξίωται; τοῦτον οὖν τὸν ἐκεῖθεν ἐξουσίας τετυχηκότα οὐ θεραπεύσει δικαίως ὁ σέβων τὸν θεόν; οὔτε γὰρ οἷόν τε, φησὶ, „δουλεύειν“ τὸν αὐτὸν πλείοσι „κυρίοις.“ ὅρα δὴ καὶ ἐν τούτοις ὅσα συναρπάζει, δεόμενα οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτου ἐξετάσεως ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπιστήμης βαθυτέρων καὶ ἀποῤῥητοτέρων περὶ τῆς τῶν ὅλων πραγμάτων διοικήσεως. τὸ γὰρ πάντα κατὰ γνώμην διοικεῖσθαι τοῦ θεοῦ πῶς λέγεται, ἐξεταστέον, καὶ πότερον τὸ διοικεῖσθαι φθάνει καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ ἁμαρτανόμενα ἢ μή. εἰ μὲν γὰρ φθάνει τὸ διοικεῖσθαι καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ ἁμαρτανόμενα οὐ μόνον ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀλλὰ καὶ δαίμοσι καὶ εἴ τι ἄλλο τῶν ἔξω σωμάτων πέφυκεν ἁμαρτάνειν, ὁράτω τὴν ἀτοπίαν ὁ τοῦτο λέγων τοῦ πάντα κατὰ γνώμην διοικεῖσθαι τοῦ θεοῦ· ἀκολουθεῖ γὰρ τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τὰ ἁμαρτανόμενα καὶ πάντα τὰ ἀπὸ κακίας κατὰ γνώμην διοικεῖσθαι τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅπερ οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστι τῷ οὐ κωλύοντος τοῦ θεοῦ γίνεται· εἰ δὲ καὶ κυρίως τις ἀκούοι τοῦ διοικεῖσθαι, διοικεῖσθαι μὲν λέγει τὰ ἀπὸ κακίας διοικούμενα (δηλονότι πάντα κατὰ γνώμην διοικεῖται τοῦ θεοῦ), καὶ οὐ παρανομεῖ εἰς τὴν διοίκησιν τοῦ θεοῦ πᾶς ἁμαρτάνων. τὸ δ᾿ ὅμοιον καὶ περὶ προνοίας διασταλτέον καὶ λεκτέον ὅτι τὸ πᾶσα ἐξ ἐκείνου πρόνοια σημαίνει μέν τι ἀληθὲς, ὅτε ἡ πρόνοια σπουδαῖόν ἐστιν· εἰ δ᾿ ἁπαξαπλῶς πάντα τὰ γινόμενα (κατὰ) πρόνοιαν εἶναι φήσομεν, κἂν κακῶς τι γίνηται, ψεῦδος ἔσται τὸ πᾶσα ἐξ ἐκείνου πρόνοια· εἰ μὴ ἄρα καὶ τὰ κατ᾿ ἐπακολούθησιν τῶν ἐκ προνοίας θεοῦ λέγοι τις εἶναι ἐκ προνοίας θεοῦ. ἀποφαίνεται δὲ καὶ ὅ τι περ ἂν ᾖ ἐν τοῖς ολοις, εἴτε θεοῦ ἔργον εἴτ᾿ ἀγγέλων εἴτε ἄλλων δαιμόνων εἴτε ἡρώων, πάντα ταῦτα ἔχει νόμον ἐκ τοῦ μεγίστου θεοῦ, καὶ οὐκ ἀληθῆ γε λόγον ἀποφαίνεται. οὐδὲ γὰρ τὰ παρανομοῦντα ἑπόμενα νόμῳ τῷ ἀπὸ μεγίστου θεοῦ παρανομεῖ. παρανομεῖν δὲ ὁ λόγος δείκνυσιν οὐ μόνον ἀνθρώπους φαύλους ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς φαύλους δαίμονας καὶ τοὺς φαύλους ἀγγέλους.
pass_a_gloss: On account of the many things said by us above about Jesus there is no need now to repeat (παλιλλογέω) in reply to: 'that then they are clearly (σαφῶς) refuted/convicted (διελέγχω) revering (σέβω) not a god, but not even a demon, but a corpse (νεκρός)'. Leaving this aside (παραλείπω) at once (αὐτίκα) for this reason, let us see Celsus's next sayings (λέξεις), in which he says: 'But first I will ask (ἐρήσομαι): why must demons not be served (θεραπευτέον)? Are not all things administered/governed (διοικέω) according to the purpose/will (γνώμη) of God, and all providence (πρόνοια) from him? And whatever there may be in the universe (τὰ ὅλα), whether work (ἔργον) of God or of angels (ἄγγελοι) or of other demons or of heroes, do not all these have a law (νόμος) from the greatest (μέγιστος) God, and over each has been appointed (τάσσω), having obtained by lot (λαγχάνω) power (δύναμις), whoever has been deemed worthy (ἀξιόω)? This one then, who has obtained (τυγχάνω) authority (ἐξουσία) from there, will not the one revering God justly (δικαίως) serve?' For neither is it possible, he says, for the same [man] 'to serve as slave (δουλεύω)' many 'lords/masters (κύριοι)'. See then also in these how many things he snatches up (συναρπάζω), needing no easily despised (εὐκαταφρόνητος) examination (ἐξέτασις) but also knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) of deeper (βαθύτερα) and more secret (ἀπορρητότερα) things about the administration (διοίκησις) of the affairs of the universe. For how the 'all things are administered according to the will of God' is said must be examined, and whether the administering reaches (φθάνω) also to the things sinned (τὰ ἁμαρτανόμενα) or not. For if the administering reaches also to the things sinned, not only among men but also demons and if anything else of those outside bodies (ἔξω σωμάτων) is by nature (φύω) to sin, let the one saying this see the absurdity (ἀτοπία) of the 'all things are administered according to the will of God'; for it follows (ἀκολουθέω) from the argument that also the sins and all the things from vice (κακία) are administered according to the will of God, which is not the same as 'it happens with God not preventing (κωλύω)'. And if someone hears (ἀκούω) 'being administered' properly/strictly (κυρίως), he says that the things from vice are administered (since evidently all things are administered according to the will of God), and every sinner does not transgress (παρανομέω) against the administration of God. And the like must be distinguished (διαστέλλω) about providence too, and it must be said that the 'all providence from him' signifies something true when the providence is a good/excellent thing (σπουδαῖον); but if simply (ἁπαξαπλῶς) we shall say that all things happening are according to providence, even if something happens badly (κακῶς), the 'all providence from him' will be false (ψεῦδος); unless perhaps someone should say that also the things by way of consequence (ἐπακολούθησις) of the things from God's providence are from God's providence. And he declares (ἀποφαίνομαι) also 'whatever there may be in the universe, whether work of God or of angels or of other demons or of heroes, all these have a law from the greatest God', and he declares no true account. For neither do the things transgressing, following (ἕπομαι) the law from the greatest God, transgress. And reason/the argument (λόγος) shows not only base (φαῦλοι) men transgressing but also the base demons and the base angels.
pass_b_english: In view of the many things we have said earlier about Jesus, there is no need now to repeat ourselves in answer to this: “So then they themselves are clearly convicted of worshipping not a god, nor even a demon, but a corpse.” Passing this over at once for that reason, let us look at Celsus’s next words, in which he says: “But first I will ask: why should demons not be served? Are not all things governed according to the will of God, and is not all providence from him? And whatever there is in the universe, whether the work of God, or of angels, or of other demons, or of heroes, do not all these things have a law from the greatest God? And has not whoever was deemed worthy been appointed over each thing, having received a power by lot? Shall not, then, the one who worships God rightly serve this being, who has obtained his authority from that source?” “For it is not possible,” he says, “for the same man to serve many masters” (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13).

Notice, then, how much he takes for granted even in these words, matters that need no slight examination, and knowledge as well of deeper and more secret truths about the government of the whole universe. For we must examine in what sense it is said that all things are governed according to the will of God, and whether this governing extends to sins as well, or not. If the governing extends to sins as well, not only among men but also among demons and any other being outside the body whose nature can sin, let the one who says this see how absurd it is to say that all things are governed according to the will of God. For it follows from the argument that sins too, and all that comes from wickedness, are governed according to the will of God; and this is not the same as saying that they happen while God does not prevent them. And if someone takes “being governed” in its proper sense, he is saying that the things that come from wickedness are governed (since, of course, all things are governed according to the will of God); and then no one who sins transgresses against God’s government.

The same distinction must be drawn about providence. We must say that “all providence is from him” means something true when the providence is good. But if we say, without qualification, that everything that happens is according to providence, even when something happens wickedly, then “all providence is from him” will be false; unless perhaps someone were to say that what follows as a consequence of what comes from God’s providence is also from God’s providence.

He also declares that “whatever there is in the universe, whether the work of God, or of angels, or of other demons, or of heroes, all these things have a law from the greatest God”; and what he declares is not true. For those who transgress do not transgress while following the law that comes from the greatest God. And reason shows that not only wicked men transgress, but also the wicked demons and the wicked angels.

choices.choice: The first quoted sentence is Celsus’s (‘worshipping not a god, nor even a demon, but a corpse’); ‘a god’ is lowercase because it is Celsus’s generic word. In Celsus’s long question θεός is his supreme God (‘the greatest God’), so ‘God’ is capitalised, as both writers mean the highest being. γνώμη rendered ‘will’; διοικεῖσθαι ‘be governed’, διοίκησις ‘government’. ‘For it is not possible ... many masters’: Celsus’s echo of Jesus’s saying (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13, ‘no one can serve two masters’), with πλείοσι (‘many’) for δυσί (‘two’); Origen defers his answer on this saying to Book 8 (as he says at 7.70). συναρπάζει: ‘takes for granted’, literally ‘snatches up’ premises without proof. εἴ τι ἄλλο τῶν ἔξω σωμάτων: literally ‘anything else of those outside bodies’; rendered ‘any other being outside the body’, since Origen may mean beings not in human bodies rather than wholly bodiless ones. The sentence εἰ δὲ καὶ κυρίως ... πᾶς ἁμαρτάνων is a reductio: if ‘governed’ is taken strictly, sinners never transgress against God’s government; the parenthesis gives the premise. (κατὰ) πρόνοιαν: Koetschau’s supplement, followed. φαῦλοι rendered ‘wicked’ to match 7.69.
Celsus's quote: 'they are clearly convicted' -> 'they themselves are clearly convicted' (αὐτοί was dropped)
'call for no slight examination, but for knowledge' -> 'need no slight examination, and knowledge as well' (ἀλλὰ καί: knowledge in addition, not instead)
'and that no one who sins transgresses' -> '; and then no one who sins transgresses' (καὶ οὐ παρανομεῖ is the consequence, not part of what 'he is saying')
'consequence of the works of God's providence' -> 'consequence of what comes from God's providence' (τῶν ἐκ προνοίας; 'works' was added)
Matthew 6:24 / Luke 16:13 allusion confirmed (two masters; Celsus has 'many')
